```{r setup}
library(ggplot2)

ink   <- "#23272f"
accent <- "#3b5169"
soft   <- "#a9b7c6"
flag   <- "#a5342a"
paper  <- "#faf9f6"

deck_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
  theme(
    plot.background  = element_rect(fill = paper, color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = paper, color = NA),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text  = element_text(color = ink, size = 16),
    plot.title = element_text(color = ink, face = "bold", size = 18)
  )
```

## Most of every AI-token dollar pays for AI's own mistakes {.center}

::: {.hook-stat}
For every **\$1** spent on AI tokens, **18 cents** creates user-facing value.
**44 cents** pays to fix bugs the AI itself introduced.
:::

```{r fig-token-spend}
#| fig-height: 3.6
df <- data.frame(
  category = c("Value created", "Fixing AI bugs", "Everything else"),
  cents = c(18, 44, 38)
)
df$category <- factor(df$category, levels = rev(df$category))
df$fill <- c(soft, flag, soft)[match(df$category, rev(c("Value created", "Fixing AI bugs", "Everything else")))]

ggplot(df, aes(category, cents, fill = category)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(cents, "¢")), hjust = -0.15, size = 6, color = ink) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Value created" = soft, "Fixing AI bugs" = flag, "Everything else" = soft)) +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  ylim(0, 55) +
  deck_theme +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold"))
```

::: {.cite}
Survey of ~2,500 companies, cited in the source article.
:::

## Agentic AI is repeating a known structural trap

- Consulting extracted returns beyond the value it created by fostering
  **dependency**, not by fraud.
- The pattern is structural: rational, incremental delegation compounds into
  a dependency that is expensive to reverse once entrenched.
- Agentic AI is running the same play, faster, and at three nested levels:
  individual, organizational, societal.

## Roadmap

1. The original con — how management consulting did this first
2. The next big con — how agentic AI repeats it, faster
3. The cost, at three levels: individual, organizational, societal
4. Two dead ends, and a third path

## The original con extracted value from dependency, not fraud

Mazzucato & Collington, *The Big Con* (2023): clients who outsource a
strategic function for years lose the internal expertise needed to judge
whether the advice they're buying is any good — which is exactly what keeps
them buying it.

No cynicism required. No negligence required. Just repeated delegation
running its natural course.

## The mechanism: the less you row, the less you steer

:::

> "The less \[an organization\] rows, the less it learns, the less
> productive it becomes: the less it can steer." — Mazzucato & Collington

## Comparative advantage is rational — until it eats identity-defining work

Outsourcing peripheral tasks (payroll, tax filing, IT support) is a
defensible specialization decision. The trap opens when the same logic
reaches the **strategic, identity-defining work**: a student's thinking, a
company's strategy, a government's policymaking.

With agentic AI, delegated agency doesn't even land with another
accountable party — it lands with a system that has none.

## The same structural logic, one level faster

```{r table-parallel}
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

parallel_df <- data.frame(
  Mechanism = c(
    "Dependency built via",
    "Pricing dynamic",
    "Who bears the risk",
    "Advisor conflict of interest"
  ),
  Consulting = c(
    "Years-long strategic engagements",
    "Fee structures reward repeat engagements",
    "Client's eroded ability to evaluate advice",
    "Consultants advise on their own future scope"
  ),
  `Agentic AI` = c(
    "Deep tool/workflow integration in months",
    "Below-cost pricing to capture market share",
    "Organization's eroded ability to evaluate output",
    "Same firms now sell AI-adoption advisory too"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(parallel_df, align = "l") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 20, full_width = TRUE) |>
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, color = ink) |>
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "22%")
```

## Subsidized pricing today is designed to become lock-in tomorrow

AI services are currently priced well below the true cost of delivery, the
same playbook early cloud and SaaS vendors used to build integration depth
before raising prices. GitHub Copilot's move to usage-based billing is an
early instance, not an outlier.

Goldman Sachs forecasts a **24x** increase in token consumption by 2030 —
compressing the price decline vendors are counting on to offset it.

## Real-world costs are already landing

```{r table-costs}
costs_df <- data.frame(
  Organization = c("Uber", "Microsoft", "Salesforce"),
  Signal = c(
    "Exhausted its entire annual AI coding budget in 4 months",
    "Cut internal AI coding licenses ~6 months after mandating adoption",
    "Expects to pay Anthropic roughly $300M in 2026 alone"
  )
)

kable(costs_df, align = "l") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 22, full_width = TRUE) |>
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, color = ink) |>
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "20%")
```

At some firms, AI token spend already equals **10%** of total labor costs.

## Vendors are reframing AI from augmentation to replacement

Software budgets are smaller and less strategic than payroll budgets, so
recasting AI as **labor replacement** implies a far larger addressable
market than "augmentation" ever did.

The firms best positioned to advise clients on this transition are the same
consultancies that drove the original outsourcing wave — and that have no
structural incentive to build the internal capability that would make
follow-on engagements unnecessary.

## Individual cost: cognitive debt replaces independent thinking

Prolonged AI assistance can leave a blank page feeling not just
uncomfortable, but daunting.

- RCTs: brief AI assistance impairs subsequent unaided performance, and
  participants stop trying sooner (**hedonic adaptation**).
- A 2027 study: measurably lower neural connectivity in participants who
  used AI to write essays — researchers call the pattern **cognitive
  debt**.
- ~2,000 professionals: most say AI "did most of the thinking," and the
  resulting ideas didn't feel fully their own.

## Organizational cost: the oversight tax

Organizations pay for **both** the AI system and a human reviewer, while
that reviewer's independent judgment quietly erodes — a **safety-net
effect** documented in AI-assisted medical screening.

The organization ends up paying twice for a review that increasingly
rubber-stamps rather than interrogates. Reported productivity gains
overstate the case; the accountability those gains are meant to justify is
hollower than it looks.

## Societal cost: accountability sinks and geopolitical dependency

"Human in the loop" was meant to mean a human who can challenge the AI and
is accountable for the result. In practice it often means a human who
approves output under time pressure — an **accountability sink**: present
to absorb blame, not to catch errors.

```{r fig-compute}
#| fig-height: 3.2
compute_df <- data.frame(
  region = c("US + China", "Rest of world"),
  share = c(90, 10)
)
compute_df$region <- factor(compute_df$region, levels = rev(compute_df$region))

ggplot(compute_df, aes(region, share, fill = region)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.55, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(share, "%")), hjust = -0.2, size = 6, color = ink) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("US + China" = flag, "Rest of world" = soft)) +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  ylim(0, 100) +
  labs(title = "Share of global AI compute capacity") +
  deck_theme +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold"))
```

June 2026: the US government ordered Anthropic to suspend its most advanced
models for all foreign nationals worldwide — with no notice, and no
recourse for the organizations depending on them.

## Banning AI and adopting it uncritically are both dead ends

**Ban it outright.** Cedes the field to whoever is least inclined to
exercise restraint, and forfeits real benefits (medicine, research,
education).

**Adopt it uncritically.** Lets vendor roadmaps and market incentives
decide how deeply AI penetrates cognitive and democratic life by default —
which is itself a choice, just an unowned one.

## The third path: ask, at every task, what AI is doing to your agency

```{r table-third-path}
path_df <- data.frame(
  Level = c("Individual", "Organizational", "Societal"),
  `Risk if unmanaged` = c(
    "Cognitive debt; atrophy of independent judgment",
    "Institutional memory loss; oversight tax",
    "Accountability sinks; single-vendor geopolitical dependency"
  ),
  `Deliberate countermeasure` = c(
    "Keep override authority; ask if AI is building capacity or replacing it",
    "Document, mentor, rotate staff; no single-vendor lock-in",
    "Legal standard: reviewers must explain and defend, not just approve"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(path_df, align = "l") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 19, full_width = TRUE) |>
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, color = ink) |>
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "16%")
```
